title: Donald Trump orders the assassination of a U.S. citizen
description_short: Donald Trump orders the assassination of a U.S. citizen
description_medium: On September 3, 2020, U.S. Marshals killed Michael Forest Reinoehl, who was wanted after a fatal shooting that he said was self-defense. Trump later said on Fox News that he had ordered the Marshals to “go get him.” Witnesses disputed the initial account of a shootout, and the county coroner ruled the death a homicide.
description_long: U.S. Marshals killed Michael Forest Reinoehl on September 3, 2020, after he became a suspect in the shooting death of a member of a white nationalist group; Reinoehl had said that earlier shooting was self-defense. On September 12, Donald Trump told Fox News that he had ordered the Marshals to “go get him,” and added that the killing was how it had to be. Trump File later quoted him describing the operation as taking 15 minutes. Initial accounts from Trump and law enforcement described a shootout or suggested Reinoehl shot himself. Witnesses said he was unarmed and walking to his car when officers opened fire, and the Thurston County coroner ruled the death a homicide. The account does not establish that Trump gave a specific unlawful order or adjudicate the circumstances of the shooting; it documents his public claim of directing the Marshals and the conflicting accounts of the killing. The event raised questions about presidential statements concerning the use of lethal force against a suspect and the transparency of the operation. The charged title uses “assassination,” but this description distinguishes the source’s characterization from the established record of a fatal federal operation and Trump’s later remarks.

title: Trump: Kash Patel ousts New York FBI field office head
description_short: Trump: Kash Patel ousts New York FBI field office head
description_medium: On March 3, 2025, James Dennehy, head of the FBI’s New York field office, told colleagues he had been directed to submit retirement papers. Reports said he had resisted efforts to scrutinize agents involved in politically sensitive cases, including January 6 investigations. The departure occurred amid turmoil at the bureau after Kash Patel became director and DOJ sought a list of those agents.
description_long: James Dennehy, a veteran FBI official and head of the bureau’s New York field office, told colleagues on March 3, 2025, that he had been directed to submit retirement papers. The Associated Press account quoted in the entry said Dennehy was not given a reason for the directive. Reports linked his departure to resistance against Justice Department efforts to scrutinize agents who had worked on politically sensitive investigations, including the January 6 cases. The episode took place during broader upheaval at the FBI after Kash Patel became director and conservative podcaster Dan Bongino was named deputy director. The Justice Department had made what the cited reporting described as a highly unusual demand for a list of agents who investigated the Capitol attack. Trump File’s author further argues that the New York office had previously been involved in politically consequential leaks, but that claim is commentary and is not needed to establish Dennehy’s departure. The available account supports describing a forced retirement amid disputes over agent scrutiny; it does not identify the official reason for the order or establish that Dennehy was dismissed for a specific act. The episode raised concerns about how the bureau handled personnel who resisted political scrutiny of investigative work.

title: NY AG Finds Trump Financial Statements Fraudulently Inflated by $2.2 Billion
description_short: NY AG Finds Trump Financial Statements Fraudulently Inflated by $2.2 Billion
description_medium: In September 2022, New York Attorney General Letitia James filed a civil fraud lawsuit alleging that Donald Trump and his company inflated asset values by as much as $2.2 billion on financial statements over roughly a decade. The supplied synopsis says a judge later found Trump liable and imposed a large monetary judgment, but the linked 2023 article covers the lawsuit before trial, not its later appellate status.
description_long: New York Attorney General Letitia James filed a civil fraud lawsuit against Donald Trump, the Trump Organization, and several family members and executives in September 2022. The complaint alleged that financial statements overstated asset values by as much as $2.2 billion over a decade, helping the company obtain favorable loan and insurance terms. The supplied synopsis says a judge later found Trump liable and imposed a judgment exceeding $450 million including interest. However, the only linked article is from August 2023 and reports the pretrial dispute over whether the case should proceed; it does not document the later judgment or subsequent appeals. Because the title and synopsis summarize both the attorney general’s allegations and later court action, and because the disposition may have changed after the cited article, the current legal outcome cannot be confirmed from the assigned source material. This record is therefore marked `needs_context` pending an updated source on the judgment and its appellate status. The description distinguishes the lawsuit’s allegations from the later liability finding and avoids presenting the monetary penalty as currently final. The case concerns alleged financial misstatements, but a current account requires a source covering the full procedural history.

title: Donald Trump tells Rick Gates that WikiLeaks isn't done yet
description_short: Donald Trump tells Rick Gates that WikiLeaks isn't done yet
description_medium: In late July or early August 2016, Donald Trump told campaign aide Rick Gates that more Democratic emails would be leaked, according to Gates’s account to Mueller investigators. Gates said Paul Manafort had earlier instructed him to contact an unnamed source periodically for updates about future leaks. The conversation followed the release of stolen Democratic National Committee emails around the party convention.
description_long: In late July or early August 2016, Donald Trump and campaign aide Rick Gates rode from Trump Tower to LaGuardia Airport. Gates later told investigators for Special Counsel Robert Mueller that Trump said “more leaks were coming,” referring to Democratic National Committee or Hillary Clinton emails. The conversation took place shortly after Russian hackers stole DNC emails, which were released during the Democratic National Convention and disrupted the party’s gathering. Gates also told investigators that campaign chairman Paul Manafort had instructed him in June to call an unnamed source periodically for updates about future leaks. The supplied account does not identify that source or establish how Trump knew additional material was coming. The reported conversation is notable because it places Trump in a discussion about anticipated disclosures while his campaign was operating amid the 2016 email releases. It is not, by itself, proof that Trump or Gates coordinated with the hackers or WikiLeaks. The record attributes the account to Gates’s statements to investigators and preserves the uncertainty around the source of his information. The event illustrates why the campaign’s awareness of forthcoming leaks became relevant to later inquiries into Russian interference and contacts around the election.

title: Trump Admin lifts sanctions on organized crime figure Dan Gertler
description_short: Trump Admin lifts sanctions on organized crime figure Dan Gertler
description_medium: On January 15, 2021, the Trump administration granted Israeli billionaire Dan Gertler a one-year special license easing U.S. sanctions. The New York Times reported that Gertler had lobbied for relief through attorney Alan Dershowitz and former FBI director Louis Freeh. Officials cited a national-security interest, while critics questioned the decision and its lack of public justification.
description_long: On January 15, 2021, the Trump administration granted a one-year special license that eased U.S. sanctions on Dan Gertler, an Israeli billionaire accused of benefiting from corruption in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The New York Times reported that Gertler had appealed directly to the Treasury Department and offered to have independent agencies monitor his businesses. His effort was initially represented by attorney Alan Dershowitz and former FBI director Louis Freeh. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin and Secretary of State Mike Pompeo advanced the process, while U.S. Ambassador David Friedman also supported Gertler’s request. The license gave Gertler access to money frozen in U.S. banks and allowed him to resume some business activity for a year. Officials cited a national-security interest in his dealings in Africa, but some State Department officials questioned whether that interest outweighed the harms alleged against him. Critics said the decision sent a message that sanctions could be eased through lobbying. The entry records the administration’s use of a special license and the competing justifications reported at the time; it does not treat the allegations against Gertler as a criminal conviction. The action raised questions about sanctions policy, transparency, and the influence of private lobbying on foreign-policy decisions.

title: Trump admin helps mortgage servicer that broke law several times
description_short: Trump admin helps mortgage servicer that broke law several times
description_medium: On July 1, 2025, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau under acting director Russell Vought ended a consent order against mortgage servicer Fay Servicing and waived alleged noncompliance. The original order addressed servicing violations, including delayed foreclosure holds, disclosures, insurance cancellation, and late fees. Fay had also been accused of violating a 2017 consent order and had paid consumer compensation and a civil penalty.
description_long: On July 1, 2025, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau under acting director Russell Vought terminated its consent order against mortgage servicer Fay Servicing and waived alleged noncompliance. The order had addressed mortgage-servicing violations, including failures to place foreclosure holds promptly, inadequate disclosures about loss-mitigation options, late cancellation of private mortgage insurance, and fees above contract limits. The CFPB also said Fay had violated a 2017 consent order covering similar conduct. Under the earlier enforcement action, the company paid $3 million in consumer compensation and a $2 million civil penalty, and it faced monitoring and compliance requirements. Vought said the company had fulfilled several of its obligations, which the CFPB used to justify ending the order. Trump File questioned whether ending oversight would leave borrowers exposed to renewed misconduct, but the available source does not document subsequent violations after the order was terminated. The decision reduced federal monitoring of a servicer that regulators had previously found out of compliance with mortgage laws. It raised concerns about the effectiveness of consumer protections when an agency removes restrictions before the public can assess whether a company has sustained compliance. This account separates the CFPB’s past findings from the source’s warning about future risk.

title: Donald Trump releases ‘The America We Deserve,' co-author says it's fiction
description_short: Donald Trump releases ‘The America We Deserve,' co-author says it's fiction
description_medium: Donald Trump released The America We Deserve, co-written with Dave Shiflett, on January 15, 2000, as a platform for his potential presidential campaign. The book supported proposals such as universal health care, a one-time wealth tax, union rights, and abortion access. In 2015, Shiflett said he wrote the book himself for money and considered it fiction.
description_long: Donald Trump released The America We Deserve on January 15, 2000. Co-written with journalist Dave Shiflett, the book was presented as a kind of manifesto for Trump’s possible presidential campaign. It advocated policies that were then described as progressive, including universal health care, a one-time 14.25% tax on wealth, support for unions, and abortion rights. The book also discussed terrorism and named Osama bin Laden, though the account says Trump did not connect the two. In 2015, Shiflett said he had taken the project because he needed the money and described it as his first work of fiction. He also said he was the only person who wrote the text, despite Trump’s name on the cover. That later comment complicates how the book should be understood as a statement of Trump’s own policy views: it was marketed under his name and linked to a potential campaign, but its credited co-author said he wrote it and regarded it as fiction. The entry records the publication, its policy content, and Shiflett’s later description without treating the book as a formal campaign platform or assuming that every proposal reflected Trump’s settled positions.

title: Donald Trump: Supporters should guard the polls, and militias stand by
description_short: Donald Trump: Supporters should guard the polls, and militias stand by
description_medium: At the September 29, 2020 presidential debate, Donald Trump declined to condemn white supremacists and right-wing militias, telling the Proud Boys to “stand back and stand by.” He also urged supporters to watch polling places closely and would not promise to accept the certified election result. The Proud Boys publicly echoed his phrase afterward.
description_long: During the first presidential debate of 2020 on September 29, Donald Trump was asked to condemn white supremacist groups and right-wing militias. After Joe Biden named the Proud Boys, Trump told them to “stand back and stand by.” The group quickly repeated the phrase on social media. When moderator Chris Wallace asked whether he would urge calm and wait for independent certification before declaring victory, Trump instead told supporters to go into polling places and watch carefully. The timeline characterized that call as voter intimidation and noted that intimidation is prohibited by law. Trump also refused to commit to accepting the election result. His statements combined encouragement for partisan poll watching with language that a militia group publicly treated as a signal. The remarks raised concerns about intimidation at polling places and the president’s willingness to respect the certification process. This account records the debate exchange and the Proud Boys’ response; it does not claim that the group’s later conduct was directed by Trump through this phrase alone. The event became a prominent example of rhetoric that placed pressure on election administration and amplified the role of armed or militant groups in political disputes.

title: Trump: Masked agents detain visa student for criticizing Israel in school newspaper
description_short: Trump: Masked agents detain visa student for criticizing Israel in school newspaper
description_medium: On March 25, 2025, masked Department of Homeland Security agents detained Rumeysa Ozturk, a Turkish doctoral student at Tufts University, near the campus. DHS said her student visa had been revoked over alleged support for Hamas but provided no evidence in the account. Reporting found that Ozturk had co-written a student newspaper op-ed criticizing Tufts’ response to pro-Palestinian protests.
description_long: Department of Homeland Security agents detained Rumeysa Ozturk, a 30-year-old Turkish doctoral student at Tufts University, on March 25, 2025. The Trump File account says masked agents waited near the university’s Interfaith Center in unmarked vehicles, surrounded and handcuffed Ozturk, and took her away without identifying themselves. Ozturk was in the United States on an F-1 student visa and was a Fulbright scholar studying child development. A DHS spokesperson said her visa had been revoked for “supporting terrorists” and alleged that she supported Hamas, but the source says the department provided no evidence. Journalists found no evidence that Ozturk had participated in pro-Palestinian campus protests. They did find a March 2024 op-ed she co-wrote in the Tufts student newspaper criticizing the university’s response to protests over Palestinian rights. Secretary of State Marco Rubio later confirmed the visa revocation and warned that student visas could be withdrawn for activism. The detention raised concerns that immigration authority was being used in response to protected political expression. This description attributes the terrorism allegation to DHS and notes that the supplied reporting did not substantiate it; it does not present the allegation as fact.

title: Trump: Michael Caputo works with Russia to improve Putin's image in the U.S.
description_short: Trump: Michael Caputo works with Russia to improve Putin's image in the U.S.
description_medium: The supplied timeline says Michael Caputo began working in Moscow in 2000 for Gazprom Media on a publicity campaign intended to improve Vladimir Putin’s image in the United States. It says Roger Stone later encouraged Caputo to move to Miami and start a public-relations firm. The entry notes that its sources still needed to be added, and the linked 2017 article does not document the 2000 work.
description_long: This entry’s supplied synopsis says Michael Caputo began working in Moscow for Gazprom Media in 2000 on a publicity effort to improve Vladimir Putin’s image in the United States. It further says that, after Caputo returned later that year, Roger Stone asked him to move to Miami Beach, where he established a public-relations firm. The linked Trump File page explicitly notes “will update with sources,” and the second link is a 2017 New York Times report about Caputo’s later role around the Trump campaign and Russia investigation. Neither assigned source provides documentation for the described 2000 employment or the specific public-relations campaign. The connection to Donald Trump is also indirect in the event as described: it concerns Caputo’s earlier career, years before he became associated with Trump’s campaign. Because the central details lack a supporting source in the assigned material, this record is marked `needs_context`. A contemporaneous source or reliable retrospective account is needed to establish Caputo’s role at Gazprom Media, the scope of the campaign, and Stone’s involvement. Until then, the synopsis should be treated as an unverified lead rather than a completed factual account.
